response.query: Which diabetes induction model (STZ dose, route, single vs multiple injections, or alloxan) and sustained hyperglycemia threshold will we use, and when will animals be randomized and treatment begin?
response.answer: We use a single high dose of STZ (45-65 mg/kg IV) for diabetes induction. Animals are randomized and treatment begins 3 days post-induction. Sustained hyperglycemia threshold is maintained at >300 mg/dL.

results.title: Streptozotocin as a tool for induction of rat models of diabetes: a practical guide - PMC
results.content: In chemically-induced models of type 1 diabetes, both single high dose of STZ [35-65 mg/kg intravenously (IV) or intraperitoneally (IP)] (Srinivasan and Ramarao, 2007[124])) and multiple injections of sub-diabetogenic low dose of STZ (15 mg/kg for 5 consecutive days IV (Rossini et al., 1977[111]) or 20 mg/kg for 5 consecutive days IP (Lukić et al., 1998[76])) are used in rats. When diabetogenic doses of STZ (45-65 mg/kg) is injected to male white Wistar rats, a triphasic response is observed in blood glucose concentration (Junod et al., 1967[58], 1969[59]; Gajdosík et al., 1999[30]): (1) early transient hyperglycemia (2-4 h after STZ injection) probably due to adrenaline response and sudden breakdown of liver glycogen without a parallel increase in serum insulin; (2) transient hypoglycemia (7-10 h after STZ injection) due to increased serum insulin because of insulin release from necrotizing β-cells but without a decrease in pancreatic insulin content; (3) stable hyperglycemia (24 h after STZ injection and onwards); in this phase, frank diabetes characterized by fasting permanent hyperglycemia, relative hypoinsulinemia (i.e., serum insulin was comparable with fasted normal animals but low related to coexisting hyperglycemia), polyuria, glycosuria, and marked (>90 %) decrease in pancreatic insulin content (Junod et al., 1969[59]). Another report in male and female mice indicates that injecting a single dose of STZ in non-fasted animals can successfully induce diabetes (de la Garza-Rodea et al., 2010[18]). Susceptibility to the diabetogenic effect of STZ is inversely related to animal age; in male Wistar rats aged 25-50 days, higher doses of STZ are needed to induce diabetes successfully in younger rats (Masiello et al., 1975[84], 1979[85]). In a study in male Wistar rats, mortality rates were 1 out of 8, 2 out of 8, and 8 out of 8 during 2-3 days following 50, 60, and 70 mg/kg STZ injection (IV) to overnight-fasted animals (Gajdosík et al., 1999[30]). Measures to prevent early hypoglycemia-related mortality following STZ injection in rats include providing access to food soon after the injection (Junod et al., 1967[58], 1969[59]), administration of glucose (Fischer and Rickert, 1975[25]; Bar-On et al., 1976[6]; Babu and Srinivasan, 1997[4]; Palsamy and Subramanian, 2011[97]) or sucrose (Tesch and Allen, 2007[133]; Ramzy et al., 2014[103]) solutions in the first 24-48 h after the injection, administration of the drug to fed animals (Gajdosík et al., 1999[30]), and using the anomer-equilibrated solutions of STZ (de la Garza-Rodea et al., 2010[18]).

results.title: STZ-Induced Diabetes Model – Protocol
results.content: In this particular study, animals to be tested further will be randomly assigned to one of 5 groups: three test compound groups (each receiving one of three doses), vehicle only, and positive control (gabapentin). The behavior test assays the sensory response of the animals to mechanical stimulation (paw withdrawal threshold), which will then be compared to the animalsʼ pre-diabetes level and to their post-diabetes/pre-drug level of threshold stimulation. The animals are tested to determine mechanical paw withdrawal threshold using the up/down technique (Dixon, 1980; cf. Following induction of diabetes (see Design, above), only animals that have at least a 25% decrease in withdrawal threshold compared to baseline will receive a test compound. Post-treatment testing of mechanical paw withdrawal threshold will be performed 30 min following dosing.

results.title: Alloxan-Induced Diabetes Mellitus - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics
results.content: Alloxan induced diabetes mellitus is defined as a condition resulting from the administration of alloxan, a pyrimidine derivative that induces diabetes in experimental models, leading to various reproductive and developmental issues through mechanisms such as oxidative stress and DNA damage in pancreatic beta cells. Alloxan induced diabetes has repeatedly been shown to reduce lipogenesis in rat liver concomitant with decreased activity of acetyl CoA carboxylase which led to the assumption that insulin is required for the synthesis of acetyl CoA carboxylase even though the actual amount of enzyme was not measured. The role of insulin in regulating the amount of acetyl CoA carboxylase in liver was re-examined using alloxan treated rats and the authors observed that although there was a decrease in the quantity of the active cytoplasmic form of acetyl CoA carboxylase in the liver of alloxan induced acute diabetic rats, there was a corresponding increase in the quantity of relatively inactive forms of the enzyme associated with mitochondria (Roman-Lopez and Allred 1987). The early use of pancreatectomy to produce diabetic animals for the study of insulin secretion and diabetes was initially superseded by alloxan, which reduces production and secretion of insulin and glucagon by damaging pancreatic beta cells, but does not impede secretion of other pancreatic products. In rat, mouse, rabbit, and dog, alloxan-induced diabetes is a model for type-1 diabetes because a severe insulin deficiency is produced. Additionally, placental angiogenesis was higher in placentas from alloxan-induced diabetic rats. Placentas from severe STZ-induced diabetic rats showed that the junctional area is increased whereas labyrinth area is decreased in this organ, and cellularity in both areas is increased compared with mildly diabetic or normoglycemic rats [73]. Additionally, placental angiogenesis was higher in placentas from alloxan-induced diabetic rats. However, alloxan is more likely to induce type I (lack of insulin) than type II (insulin resistance) diabetes since it can destroy β-cells [51]. Streptozotocin and alloxan cause similar changes, and additionally the *spontaneously* diabetic BB Wistar rat shows virtually identical patterns of tissue antioxidant enzyme changes.50 Furthermore, these alterations are preventable by insulin treatment.10,50,188,189 The common mechanism of increased oxidative stress is, therefore, diabetes (hyperglycemia) and not its mode of induction.
